reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard medical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is diagnosed clinically using criteria that include multiple cafe-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, characteristic bony lesions, and an affected first-degree relative
Cafe-au-lait macules and axillary or inguinal freckling are usually the earliest features in NF1
Optic pathway gliomas are a recognised childhood complication and warrant ophthalmological and imaging surveillance
Plexiform neurofibromas can be disfiguring and carry a risk of malignant transformation
Neurofibromatosis type 2 is distinct, typically presenting with bilateral vestibular schwannomas causing hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance problems
NF1 is caused by mutations in the NF1 gene encoding neurofibromin, a tumour suppressor regulating RAS signalling; NF2 involves the NF2 gene encoding merlin
Both are autosomal dominant with high penetrance, variable expressivity, and a high de novo mutation rate
Learning difficulties, hypertension, and skeletal complications such as scoliosis are common in NF1
reference.pathophysiology: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 gene, which encodes neurofibromin, a GTPase-activating protein that downregulates RAS signalling; loss of neurofibromin increases RAS-pathway activity and predisposes to tumour formation in neural crest-derived tissues. Neurofibromatosis type 2 results from mutations in the NF2 gene encoding merlin (schwannomin), another tumour suppressor, leading characteristically to schwannomas and meningiomas. Both disorders are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner but frequently arise de novo, and tumour development typically follows a second somatic hit inactivating the remaining normal allele, consistent with the two-hit tumour suppressor model.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment against established diagnostic criteria, supported by NF1 or NF2 molecular testing when needed
Ophthalmological examination including slit-lamp for Lisch nodules and optic pathway assessment
Magnetic resonance imaging for suspected central or peripheral nervous system tumours
Blood pressure monitoring for hypertension including phaeochromocytoma and renal artery stenosis
Audiological evaluation and brain imaging for suspected NF2
redFlags: New or rapidly enlarging, painful, or firm masses suggesting malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour and needing urgent evaluation
Visual changes indicating optic pathway glioma progression
Hypertension that may reflect phaeochromocytoma or renovascular disease
Progressive hearing loss or neurological signs from vestibular schwannomas or other tumours in NF2
reference.prognosis: Most people with NF1 have a good quality of life, but morbidity and reduced life expectancy relate to tumour complications, particularly malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours and vascular disease; NF2 prognosis depends on the burden and location of nervous system tumours.
pitfalls: Attributing multiple cafe-au-lait macules alone to NF1 without considering mimics such as Legius syndrome
Failing to institute malignancy surveillance for changing plexiform neurofibromas
Overlooking hypertension and its treatable secondary causes
Missing NF2 in a young adult with unilateral or bilateral hearing loss
management: There is no cure, so care centres on structured lifelong surveillance for the many complications, coordinated by a specialist neurofibromatosis service
Monitor children with regular clinical review, blood pressure checks and ophthalmological and visual assessment for optic pathway glioma
Treat symptomatic or progressive inoperable plexiform neurofibromas with a MEK inhibitor (selumetinib) and refer for surgery where appropriate
Investigate and manage malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour promptly with oncological and surgical care when a plexiform lesion becomes painful or rapidly enlarging
Screen for and manage hypertension, including secondary causes such as phaeochromocytoma and renal artery stenosis
Address skeletal, learning and psychosocial complications with orthopaedic, educational and psychological support
For neurofibromatosis type 2, undertake audiological monitoring and MRI surveillance for vestibular schwannomas with hearing-preservation strategies
Offer genetic counselling and family assessment given autosomal dominant inheritance
